questions.question: What is the primary way energy is transferred to the surroundings when a fuel is burned?
options: By cooling down the immediate environment
By heating the surroundings
By absorbing light from the room
By creating a vacuum

questions.question: How can we compare the amounts of energy transferred by different fuels in a school laboratory?
options: By measuring the sound level of each burning fuel
By heating a volume of water in a boiling tube with each fuel
By weighing the ashes left behind on a balance
By checking the colour of the flame with a light sensor

questions.question: To make a fair comparison between the energy transferred by different fuels, what must be kept the same for each measurement?
options: The mass of the fuel used
The shape of the boiling tube holder
The room temperature of the laboratory
The brand of matches used to light them

questions.question: In an experiment comparing fuels by heating water, which variables regarding the water must be kept constant for each test?
options: Its pH and clarity
Its density and salt concentration
Its starting temperature and volume
Its depth and surface area in the beaker

questions.question: When looking at a cooling curve graph of a substance, how can you identify where a change of state is occurring?
options: The line becomes a flat horizontal plateau
The line goes straight up vertically
The line begins to curve downwards more steeply
The line stops completely and disappears

questions.question: What happens to energy as a hot substance cools, and what state change might occur?
options: It transfers energy into the surroundings and may condense or freeze
It absorbs energy from the surroundings and may melt or boil
It destroys energy and may sublimate into gas
It keeps its energy constant and may expand in volume

questions.question: As a warm liquid cools down, how is the release of energy to its surroundings observed?
options: An increase in the mass of the liquid
A decrease in the temperature of the substance
An increase in the volume of the substance
A sudden change in the colour of the liquid

questions.question: What is the main observable effect on the surroundings during an exothermic chemical reaction?
options: The temperature of the surroundings decreases
The temperature of the surroundings increases
The surroundings turn into a gas
The pressure of the surroundings drops to zero

questions.question: What temperature change is observed in the surroundings during an endothermic chemical reaction?
options: The temperature remains exactly the same
The temperature increases rapidly
The temperature decreases
The temperature fluctuates up and down randomly

questions.question: During an exothermic reaction, how is energy transferred?
options: From the surroundings to the products
From the reactants to the surroundings
From the products to the reactants
From the atmosphere to the container

questions.question: How is energy transferred in an endothermic reaction?
options: From the surroundings to the products
From the products to the surroundings
From the reactants to the beaker
From the products to the reactants

questions.question: Which of the following physical changes are classified as endothermic processes?
options: Freezing and condensing
Melting, evaporation, and boiling
Condensing and melting
Freezing and boiling

questions.question: Why are condensing and freezing described as exothermic processes?
options: They absorb heat energy from the surroundings
They release energy to the surroundings
They increase the temperature of the substance itself
They require continuous heating to take place

questions.question: In the UK, over half of the electricity is generated from which group of energy sources?
options: Coal, oil, and natural gas
Nuclear power and biomass
The Sun, wind, and falling water
Geothermal and waves only

questions.question: Which fuels do many power stations in the UK burn to heat water into steam?
options: Coal and wood
Natural gas and oil
Uranium and hydrogen
Biomass and charcoal

questions.question: In a steam-driven power station, what is the correct sequence of components used to produce electricity?
options: Steam pushes turbines, which drive electric generators
Steam heats generators, which spin the solar panels
Steam cools the turbines, which power the furnace
Steam turns into water, which directly powers the cables

questions.question: Which of these fossil fuels is no longer used in UK power stations to generate electricity?
options: Natural gas
Oil
Coal
Petroleum

questions.question: Which group of fuels all produce greenhouse gases and pollutants when they are burned?
options: Wind, solar, and falling water
Natural gas, oil, waste, and wood
Hydrogen, helium, and pure oxygen
Geothermal, waves, and tides

questions.question: Why are renewable energy resources defined as resources that will not run out?
options: Because they are replenished more quickly than we use them up
Because they are stored in infinite underground reservoirs
Because we only use a tiny fraction of them each year
Because they are created by chemical reactions inside turbines

questions.question: How do solar panels differ from wind turbines and steam-driven generators when producing electricity?
options: They produce electricity without using electric generators
They must burn oil to start working
They require steam to turn their internal coils
They use falling water to spin magnets
